paras: The Third Creek riot was a fight between whites and Black men at Third Creek station on the Western North Carolina Railroad on Saturday, March 11, 1882. About a hundred people took part, some with pistols and shotguns, and several Black men were badly but not fatally shot. A Salisbury militia company ended the fighting and jailed twenty-four rioters, and a Raleigh dispatch carried the story to papers across the country under headlines such as "Negroes Rioting in North Carolina."

Third Creek was a station on the Western North Carolina Railroad between Salisbury and Statesville; one version of the Raleigh wire placed it in Catawba county, while the local account named no county. The local account came from Hall Caldwell, who had just returned from a trip on the railroad and reported what he had learned to the Concord Sun.

According to the Concord Sun, the trouble began when a Black man attacked a young white man who had recently returned from Texas. When the white man defended himself, several Black men came to their friend's aid, and whites "seeing this, also took a hand" until the fight became a riot. The Sun described "a lively engagement with pistols and shot guns" among about a hundred people.

A Salisbury militia company, called the Salisbury Rifles in one reprint and the Rowan Guards in another, was telegraphed for and left at once for the scene. Several Black men were badly but not fatally shot; no white casualties and no deaths were reported.

The militia arrested twenty-four rioters, carried them to Salisbury and put them in jail, though the reports do not give the race of those arrested. The wire said only that troops "arrested many of the rioters and placed them in jail." No report of charges, a trial or any other outcome for the arrested men appears in the coverage.

The story spread mainly through a Raleigh dispatch dated March 12, which said a Black man attacked a white man, "more negroes took part," and whites came to the man's aid. The Savannah Morning News headed it "Negroes Rioting in North Carolina," the Waco Daily Examiner "Suppressing a Race Riot in North Carolina," and the New-York Tribune "A Southern Riot Quelled by Troops." A shorter version naming Catawba county, which the St. Paul Daily Globe cut to "The negroes attacked the white men," appeared in Wheeling, St. Paul and later in Tennessee and Rhode Island.

Northern news columns cut the story further, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer calling it a riot "growing out of a fight between one of each color" and the Maysville Evening Bulletin a riot "requiring the interposition of military." Every version came from white sources and told the start of the fight from the white side, and only the North Carolina reprints of the Concord Sun mentioned that Black men had been shot. Weekly papers kept reprinting the dispatch until late March, sometimes with errors: the Winston Western Sentinel printed "Fully 1,000," and another reprint moved the riot to Monday and "near Raleigh."

Most reports put about one hundred people in the riot, but two reprints of the same Raleigh dispatch say 1,000, probably a printing error since the local account also says a hundred. The March 12 dispatch's "yesterday" and the Weekly Clarion's "on the 11th" fix the date as Saturday, March 11, while later reprints said Sunday or Monday.

accounts.label: Raleigh wire
accounts.gist: About one hundred whites and Black men rioted at Third Creek after a Black man attacked a white man and more Black men joined in; whites came to the man's aid, and troops arrested many and jailed them.

accounts.label: Concord Sun (Hall Caldwell)
accounts.gist: A hundred people fought with pistols and shotguns at Third Creek station after a Black man attacked a young white man back from Texas; a Salisbury militia company came, arrested twenty-four and jailed them at Salisbury, and several Black men were badly but not fatally shot.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Raleigh dispatch nearly verbatim, with headlines such as 'Negroes Rioting in North Carolina' (Savannah) and 'A Southern Riot Quelled by Troops' (New York), and told the white side of the start of the fight as fact.
Northern news columns cut it to a one-line brief about a riot 'growing out of a fight between one of each color' that troops put down.
North Carolina papers reprinted the Concord Sun's 'serious riot', adding the weapons, the militia, the arrests and the shooting of several Black men.

conflicts.note: The 1,000 figure appears only in two reprints of the same Raleigh dispatch that other papers printed as one hundred; the local Concord Sun also says a hundred, so 1,000 is probably a printing error.
The March 12 Raleigh dispatch says 'yesterday', which supports Saturday; the Sunday and Monday dates come from late reprints.
Two reprints of the same Concord Sun item name the company differently; both say it came from Salisbury.
